items.title: Two sum in one pass
items.prompt: Write `two_sum(nums, target)` returning the indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`, or `None`. Aim for O(n).
hints: For each number, which partner value would you need?
Keep a dict from value -> index of what you've already seen.
need = target - x; if need in seen: return (seen[need], i); then seen[x] = i
items.lesson: Trade memory for time: a dict of 'things seen so far' turns an O(n²) pair search into one O(n) pass. Check before you insert so an element never pairs with itself.
items.alternative: Sort (value, index) pairs and walk two pointers inward: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the pairs, but the idea generalises to 3-sum.
items.ts: const seen = new Map<number, number>(); if (seen.has(need)) return [seen.get(need)!, i];

items.title: Group anagrams
items.prompt: Write `group_anagrams(words)` returning a list of groups (lists) of words that are anagrams of each other. Keep words in input order inside each group and groups in order of first appearance.
hints: Anagrams look identical once you put their letters in a canonical order.
Use the sorted letters as a dict key; a defaultdict(list) collects the group.
groups[''.join(sorted(w))].append(w); return list(groups.values())
items.lesson: Grouping = pick a canonical key, then dict[key].append(item). Python dicts keep insertion order, so group order follows first appearance for free.
items.alternative: Key by a 26-count tuple (tuple(Counter(w)...)) — O(k) per word instead of O(k log k), but uglier and only worth it for long words.

items.title: First unique character
items.prompt: Write `first_unique(s)` returning the index of the first character that appears exactly once, or `-1`.
hints: Two passes: one to count, one to find.
collections.Counter(s) gives you counts in one line.
for i, ch in enumerate(s): if counts[ch] == 1: return i
items.lesson: 'Count, then scan in original order' is O(n) and keeps the ordering question separate from the counting question.
items.alternative: s.index(ch) / s.count(ch) per character is shorter but O(n²).
items.ts: const counts = new Map<string, number>(); for (const c of s) counts.set(c, (counts.get(c) ?? 0) + 1);

items.title: Top k frequent words
items.prompt: Write `top_k(words, k)` returning the `k` most frequent words, most frequent first; ties broken alphabetically.
hints: Count first, then sort the distinct words.
Sort key: higher count first, then the word itself.
sorted(counts, key=lambda w: (-counts[w], w))[:k]
items.solution:
from collections import Counter

def top_k(words, k):
    counts = Counter(words)
    return sorted(counts, key=lambda w: (-counts[w], w))[:k]
items.lesson: Sort by a tuple key to express multi-level ordering; negate a number to flip it to descending while the string stays ascending.
items.alternative: heapq.nsmallest(k, counts, key=lambda w: (-counts[w], w)) is O(n log k) — better when k ≪ n. Counter.most_common(k) doesn't break ties alphabetically.

items.title: Pair sum in a sorted list
items.prompt: `nums` is sorted ascending. Write `pair_sum(nums, target)` returning a tuple of indices `(i, j)`, `i < j`, whose values add to `target`, else `None`. O(1) extra space.
hints: Start one pointer at each end.
If the sum is too small, which pointer should move? Too big?
while i < j: s = nums[i] + nums[j]; if s == target: return (i, j); elif s < target: i += 1; else: j -= 1
items.lesson: Sorted input + pair question → converging pointers. Each step discards one candidate, so it's O(n) time and O(1) space.
items.alternative: The dict approach from two-sum also works (O(n) space) and doesn't need sorting.

items.title: Dedupe a sorted list in place
items.prompt: Write `dedupe(nums)` that removes duplicates from sorted `nums` **in place** (keep the first `k` slots unique, in order) and returns `k`. Don't build a new list.
items.tests:
def test_basic():
    a = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]
    k = dedupe(a)
    assert k == 4, f"expected 4 unique, got {k}"
    assert a[:k] == [1, 2, 3, 4], f"first k slots wrong: {a[:k]}"
def test_same_object():
    a = [5, 5]
    ref = a
    dedupe(a)
    assert a is ref and a[0] == 5, "modify the list you were given"
def test_empty():
    assert dedupe([]) == 0
def test_all_unique():
    a = [1, 2, 3]
    assert dedupe(a) == 3 and a == [1, 2, 3]
hints: One pointer reads every element, another marks where the next unique value goes.
A value is new if it differs from the last value you wrote.
w = 1; for r in range(1, len(nums)): if nums[r] != nums[w-1]: nums[w] = nums[r]; w += 1
items.lesson: Read/write pointers compact an array in place in O(n): the reader scans everything, the writer only advances when it keeps something.
items.alternative: nums[:] = dict.fromkeys(nums) is one line and also in-place from the caller's view, but uses O(n) extra memory.

items.title: Valid palindrome
items.prompt: Write `is_palindrome(s)`: True if `s` reads the same both ways considering only letters/digits and ignoring case. Use two indices, not a reversed copy.
hints: Skip characters that aren't alphanumeric from either side.
str.isalnum() and str.lower() are what you need.
while i < j: skip non-alnum with inner whiles, compare s[i].lower() != s[j].lower()
items.lesson: An if/elif chain inside one while loop avoids nested skip-loops and their off-by-one bugs: each iteration makes exactly one move.
items.alternative: t = [c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()]; return t == t[::-1] — clearer, O(n) extra space.

items.title: Max sum of k consecutive
items.prompt: Write `max_sum_k(nums, k)` returning the largest sum of any `k` consecutive numbers in O(n). Return `None` if `len(nums) < k`.
hints: Sum the first window once; don't re-sum every window.
Sliding by one: add the new element, subtract the one that fell out.
window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]; best = max(best, window)
items.lesson: Fixed window: maintain a running aggregate and update it in O(1) per step (add the entering element, remove the leaving one).
items.alternative: max(sum(nums[i:i+k]) for i in range(len(nums)-k+1)) is one line but O(n·k).
items.ts: window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]; best = Math.max(best, window);

items.title: Longest substring without repeats
items.prompt: Write `longest_unique(s)` returning the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.
hints: Grow a window to the right; shrink from the left when a repeat enters.
Remember the last index of each char; on a repeat, jump left past it — but never backwards.
if last.get(ch, -1) >= left: left = last[ch] + 1; last[ch] = i; best = max(best, i - left + 1)
items.lesson: Variable window: expand right every step, move left only as far as needed to restore the invariant ('no repeats'). Window length is i - left + 1.
items.alternative: Keep a set and `while ch in window: window.remove(s[left]); left += 1` — same O(n) amortised, easier to reason about, slightly slower.

items.title: Shortest subarray with sum ≥ target
items.prompt: All `nums` are positive. Write `min_len(nums, target)` returning the length of the shortest contiguous run whose sum is ≥ `target`, or `0` if none.
hints: Add elements on the right until the sum reaches the target.
While it's still ≥ target, record the length and drop elements from the left.
for r, x in enumerate(nums): total += x; while total >= target: best = min(best, r-l+1); total -= nums[l]; l += 1
items.lesson: A 'while' shrink inside a 'for' grow is the variable-window template. It's O(n) because each index enters and leaves the window once. Works because values are positive.
items.alternative: Prefix sums + bisect for each right end: O(n log n), also only valid for positive numbers.

items.title: Valid brackets
items.prompt: Write `valid(s)` → True if every `()[]{}` bracket in `s` is closed in the right order. Ignore other characters.
hints: The most recently opened bracket must close first — that's LIFO.
Map each closer to its opener: {')': '(', ...}.
on a closer: if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]: return False; at the end: return not stack
items.lesson: A Python list is your stack: append/pop are O(1) at the end. Two classic misses: popping an empty stack, and forgetting to check the stack is empty at the end.

items.title: Min stack
items.prompt: Write class `MinStack` with `push(x)`, `pop()` (returns the value), and `min()` — all O(1).
items.tests:
def test_min_tracks():
    s = MinStack()
    s.push(5); s.push(3); s.push(7)
    assert s.min() == 3, "min of 5,3,7"
    assert s.pop() == 7
    assert s.min() == 3
    assert s.pop() == 3
    assert s.min() == 5, "after popping 3 the min goes back to 5"
def test_duplicates():
    s = MinStack()
    s.push(2); s.push(2); s.pop()
    assert s.min() == 2, "duplicate minimums must survive one pop"
hints: Recomputing min() on every call is O(n). Store more on each push.
Push a pair (value, min_so_far) instead of just the value.
m = x if not self.items else min(x, self.items[-1][1]); self.items.append((x, m))
items.lesson: When a query must be O(1), cache its answer alongside each element at the moment you push it. The stack's LIFO order means the cache is always valid.
items.alternative: A second stack that only pushes when x <= current min — less memory when values are mostly increasing, but more edge cases (duplicates!).

items.title: Next greater element
items.prompt: Write `next_greater(nums)` returning a list where `out[i]` is the first value to the right of `nums[i]` that is larger, or `-1`. O(n).
hints: Keep a stack of indices still waiting for their answer.
When a bigger value arrives, it answers everyone smaller on top of the stack.
while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x: out[stack.pop()] = x; then stack.append(i)
items.lesson: A monotonic stack holds 'unresolved' items in decreasing order; each new item resolves the smaller ones. Every index is pushed and popped once → O(n).
items.alternative: Nested loops scanning right for each i: trivial, O(n²). Say it first, then improve.

items.title: Requests in the last 3 seconds
items.prompt: Write class `RecentCounter` with `ping(t)` (t in ms, strictly increasing) that returns how many pings happened in `[t - 3000, t]`.
items.tests:
def test_sequence():
    c = RecentCounter()
    assert c.ping(1) == 1
    assert c.ping(100) == 2
    assert c.ping(3001) == 3, "1 is still inside [1, 3001]"
    assert c.ping(3002) == 3, "1 drops out"
def test_uses_deque():
    import collections
    c = RecentCounter()
    c.ping(5)
    assert any(isinstance(v, collections.deque) for v in vars(c).values()), \
        "store pings in a collections.deque"
hints: Old pings fall out of the front, new ones join the back: a queue.
collections.deque has O(1) popleft(); list.pop(0) is O(n).
self.q.append(t); while self.q[0] < t - 3000: self.q.popleft(); return len(self.q)
items.lesson: Use deque for queues: append + popleft are O(1). Expire from the front while the oldest item is out of range — a time-based sliding window.
items.ts: JS has no deque; an array with shift() is O(n) — keep a head index instead.

items.title: Count islands
items.prompt: `grid` is a list of strings of `'1'` (land) and `'0'` (water). Write `islands(grid)` counting groups of land connected up/down/left/right.
hints: Scan every cell; each unvisited land cell starts a new island.
From that cell, visit all connected land (stack or recursion) and mark it in a `seen` set.
for each (r, c) popped: for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)): check bounds, '1', not seen
items.lesson: Counting connected components = outer scan + inner flood fill. Mark cells seen when you push them (not when you pop) so nothing is pushed twice.
items.alternative: Recursive DFS is shorter but can hit Python's recursion limit (~1000) on big grids; union-find also works and shines when cells arrive incrementally.

items.title: Shortest path in a grid
items.prompt: `grid` is a list of strings; `'#'` is a wall, `'.'` is open. Write `shortest(grid)` returning the fewest steps (4 directions) from top-left to bottom-right, or `-1`.
hints: In an unweighted graph, BFS reaches each cell first by a shortest path.
Queue (row, col, dist) in a deque; mark cells seen when you enqueue them.
q = deque([(0, 0, 0)]); while q: r, c, d = q.popleft(); if goal: return d; enqueue open unseen neighbours with d + 1
items.lesson: Shortest path with equal-cost steps → BFS with a deque. DFS finds *a* path, not the shortest. O(rows·cols).
items.alternative: With weighted edges you'd switch to Dijkstra (heapq); with 0/1 weights a deque with appendleft works (0-1 BFS).

items.title: Can A reach B?
items.prompt: `graph` is a dict `node -> list of neighbours` (directed). Write `reachable(graph, start, goal)` → bool. Graphs may contain cycles.
hints: Without a visited set, the cycle a → b → a loops forever.
Use a stack (or deque) of nodes to visit; graph.get(node, []) handles leaf nodes.
while todo: n = todo.pop(); if n == goal: return True; for m in graph.get(n, []): if m not in seen: seen.add(m); todo.append(m)
items.lesson: Every graph traversal is: frontier + visited set + 'expand neighbours'. A list frontier gives DFS, a deque with popleft gives BFS.
items.alternative: Recursive DFS with a seen set — shorter, but watch the recursion limit.

items.title: Build order (topological sort)
items.prompt: `deps` maps each task to the list of tasks it depends on. Write `order(deps)` returning a list where every task comes after its dependencies (ties: alphabetical). Raise `ValueError` on a cycle.
hints: Count unmet dependencies per task; tasks with 0 are ready.
When you finish a task, decrement its dependents; newly-0 tasks become ready. Use a heap for alphabetical ties.
If len(result) < number of tasks at the end, there's a cycle.
items.lesson: Kahn's algorithm: in-degree counts + a queue of ready nodes. Fewer outputs than nodes means a cycle. O(V + E) (plus log for the heap).
items.alternative: graphlib.TopologicalSorter(deps).static_order() is in the stdlib (3.9+) and raises CycleError — mention it, but expect to hand-write it in an interview.

items.title: Count values in a range with bisect
items.prompt: `xs` is sorted. Write `count_between(xs, lo, hi)` returning how many values `v` satisfy `lo <= v <= hi`, in O(log n).
hints: The bisect module finds insertion points in sorted lists.
bisect_left gives the first index ≥ lo; bisect_right gives the first index > hi.
return bisect_right(xs, hi) - bisect_left(xs, lo)
items.lesson: bisect_left(xs, v) = first index with xs[i] >= v; bisect_right = first index with xs[i] > v. Their difference counts a closed range.
items.alternative: sum(lo <= v <= hi for v in xs) is O(n) — fine if you only query once.

items.title: Search insert position (by hand)
items.prompt: Without `bisect`, write `search_insert(nums, target)` returning the index of `target` in sorted `nums`, or where it would be inserted to keep order.
hints: Search the half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = len(nums).
If nums[mid] < target the answer is right of mid; otherwise mid could be the answer.
while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1; else: hi = mid
items.lesson: Memorise one template: half-open [lo, hi), `while lo < hi`, `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid`. It always terminates and returns the lower bound.
items.alternative: bisect.bisect_left(nums, target) does exactly this — use it in real code.

items.title: Merge overlapping intervals
items.prompt: Write `merge(intervals)` taking `[start, end]` pairs (any order) and returning merged, sorted intervals. Touching intervals (`[1,2]`, `[2,3]`) merge.
hints: Sort by start first; then overlaps are always with the last merged interval.
Overlap if the next start ≤ the last end.
if out and s <= out[-1][1]: out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e) else: out.append([s, e])
items.lesson: Sorting first turns many interval problems into a single left-to-right sweep comparing with the last kept item. O(n log n).
items.alternative: Event sweep: +1 at each start, -1 at each end, sorted — generalises to 'max overlapping meetings'.

items.title: Leaderboard sort
items.prompt: `rows` is a list of `(name, score)`. Write `leaderboard(rows)` returning names by score descending, ties by name ascending.
items.tests:
def test_basic():
    rows = [("bo", 5), ("al", 9), ("cy", 5)]
    assert leaderboard(rows) == ["al", "bo", "cy"]
def test_input_unchanged():
    rows = [("b", 1), ("a", 2)]
    leaderboard(rows)
    assert rows == [("b", 1), ("a", 2)], "use sorted(), don't mutate input"
hints: sorted() takes a key function.
A tuple key sorts by its first element, then the second…
[name for name, _ in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))]
items.solution:
def leaderboard(rows):
    return [name for name, _ in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))]
items.lesson: sorted(xs, key=...) returns a new list; list.sort() mutates. Tuple keys give multi-level ordering; negate numbers to reverse one level.

items.question: Worst-case time complexity?
items.explanation: The inner loop runs n-1, n-2, … 1 times: n(n-1)/2 comparisons → O(n²). Starting j at i+1 halves the work but doesn't change the class.

items.code:
def common(a, b):          # len(a) = n, len(b) = m
    return [x for x in a if x in b]
items.question: `a` and `b` are lists. Time complexity — and the one-word fix?
choices: O(n·m); make b a set first
items.explanation: `x in list` scans the list: O(m) per check → O(n·m). `bs = set(b)` once makes each check O(1) on average → O(n + m).
items.ts: Same trap as arr.includes() inside a loop; use a Set.

items.question: Time complexity in terms of n?
items.explanation: Halving each iteration reaches 1 after about log₂ n steps — the same shape as binary search.

items.question: Time complexity?
items.explanation: Sort O(n log n) + one linear pass O(n): the bigger term wins → O(n log n). Sequential steps add; nested steps multiply.

items.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2])
q.append(3)
q.appendleft(0)
print(q.popleft(), q.pop())
items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: After the appends the deque is [0, 1, 2, 3]. popleft() takes from the front (0), pop() from the back (3).

items.question: "Longest substring containing at most k distinct characters." Which pattern should you reach for first?
choices: Variable sliding window + a Counter of the window
Sort the string, then two pointers
items.explanation: 'Longest/shortest contiguous run satisfying a condition' is the sliding-window signal. Grow right, shrink left while the Counter has more than k keys. O(n).

items.title: Two-sum pairs an element with itself
choices: Insert x into `seen` only after checking for its partner
Use `nums.index(target - x)` instead of the dict
items.explanation: Storing x before the lookup lets 3 find itself when target is 6. Check first, then record — the dict must only contain *earlier* elements.

items.title: Brackets that never close
items.explanation: "((" never hits a closer, so the loop finishes with openers left. The final answer must be 'stack is empty'.

items.title: Merged interval shrinks
choices: Take max(out[-1][1], e) as the new end
Sort by end instead of start
items.explanation: [2, 3] sits inside [1, 10]; overwriting the end with 3 shrinks it. The merged end is whichever end reaches further.

items.title: BFS distance in a graph
items.prompt: Arrange the lines so `dist(graph, start, goal)` returns the number of edges on the shortest path, or -1.
items.lesson: BFS template: deque of (node, distance), seen set, popleft, check goal, enqueue unseen neighbours with d + 1.

items.title: Longest run with at most k distinct
items.prompt: Arrange the lines so `longest_k(s, k)` returns the length of the longest substring with at most `k` distinct characters.
items.lesson: Counter as a window: increment on entry, decrement on exit and delete zero counts so len(window) is the number of distinct characters.
